title: How to design a case for your electronics with AI
heading: How to design a case for your electronics with AI, around the real board
description: Design a 3D printable case around your real circuit board and speaker with AI: import the board's STEP file, describe the case, check the fit, export 3MF.
summary: A smart speaker case designed by SOMA AI around the real board's STEP file and a speaker datasheet, checked with a section view and exported for printing.

video.title: A 3D Printed Case for My Smart Speaker, Designed by AI (No CAD)

chapters.label: The parts: a voice assistant board and a speaker
Import the board's STEP file and the speaker datasheet
SOMA AI places the board and builds the speaker
Check the fit: section and explode view
Add a keyhole with Mark up
Going further: a detailed smart speaker, designed in SOMA and built

answer: To design a case for your electronics with AI, give the AI the real parts: the 3D file (STEP file) of your circuit board from the manufacturer, or a datasheet with dimensions for parts that have none. In SOMA, SOMA AI places these parts as references and designs the case around them, with openings, screw posts and parameters you can change. Then you check the fit with a section view and export 3MF files for printing. Measure the important openings and print a test piece, because the AI can still get a detail wrong.
need: SOMA, free and open source, for Windows, macOS or Linux.

A sign-in for SOMA AI: a ChatGPT Plus or Pro plan, or an API key from Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI, Google Gemini, OpenRouter or OpenCode. SOMA is free, the AI runs on your plan or key. The cheapest way to start is an OpenCode Go subscription for about $10 a month.
A STEP file of your circuit board. Many manufacturers offer one on the product page; the video uses the reSpeaker XVF3800 with a XIAO ESP32S3 from Seeed Studio's wiki.
For parts without a 3D file: the datasheet with a dimensioned drawing, as a PDF. The video uses the datasheet of a Visaton FRS 5 X speaker.
A 3D printer or a printing service for the finished case.

steps.title: Get the 3D file of your board
text: Look for the 3D file of your board on the manufacturer's page, often under Resources or Downloads. It is usually a STEP file (.step or .stp). In the video it is the reSpeaker XVF3800 from Seeed Studio: four microphones, a ring of twelve LEDs, two buttons and a small XIAO ESP32S3 on the back.
Check the license on the page before you share a model that contains the file. Seeed publishes the file on its wiki under Creative Commons.

steps.title: Import the board and the datasheet
text: Start a new model and click Import at the top. Add the board's STEP file and the speaker's datasheet. SOMA puts them into the model's inputs folder, where SOMA AI can use them.
Click the STEP file in Files to look at it in the 3D view: you see the LED ring on top, and underneath the XIAO and the connectors. Back to model returns to your model.
Very detailed board files make every build slow. For the video the board file was trimmed before the import: small components became simple blocks of their size.

image.alt: The reSpeaker board in SOMA's 3D view, with a banner at the bottom: Viewing inputs/respeaker-xvf3800.step, view only, and a Back to model button

steps.title: Let SOMA AI place the parts
text: Open the SOMA AI tab and pick a model; the video uses GPT-6.1 Sol. First ask only to bring the parts into the model. SOMA AI reads the STEP file and the datasheet, measures both parts and places them: the board on top, the speaker below it, facing forward. In the video this took about 3 minutes.

The speaker has no 3D file, so SOMA AI builds it from the datasheet's dimensions and mounting holes. The structure tree lists the board with its parts, and the speaker. Both are references: see-through, used to design around, and never printed.
steps.prompt: inputs/respeaker-xvf3800.step is the board of my voice assistant, and the PDF is the datasheet of my speaker. Load the board as a reference, centered, LEDs facing up. Build the speaker from the datasheet as a reference too, below the board, facing forward.

image.alt: The structure tree lists References with the ReSpeaker XVF3800 (PCB, XIAO ESP32S3, USB-C, audio jack, buttons, LEDs, microphones) and the Visaton FRS 5 X, both see-through in the 3D view, with SOMA AI's summary on the right

steps.title: Describe the case and answer the questions
text: Now describe the case the way you would tell a friend: the shape, what must stay reachable, how it is held together and how you will print it. Name the parts that need openings and say which values you want to change later.

The last sentence asks SOMA AI to ask first. In the video it asks two questions at once: a compact size around the parts or your own dimensions, and M3 screws with heat-set inserts, captive nuts or screws into plastic. Click your answers and send them.
steps.prompt: Now design a 3D printable case for my smart speaker around them, a round tower. On top: holes above the four microphones, and a separate light ring above the LED ring that I print in white. In front: a grille for the speaker. Keep the two side buttons pressable and leave openings for the USB-C ports and the audio jack. Screw the board onto posts at its four holes and the speaker onto the front, with standard screws, and close the case with screws from below. It should print without supports. Make the wall thickness, the grille holes and the height parameters. Ask me about anything that is unclear before you start.

image.alt: SOMA AI has 2 questions: Size, with Compact fit and I have dimensions, and Fastening, with M3 heat-set inserts, M3 captive nuts and Screws into plastic

steps.title: Let SOMA AI design the case
text: Then SOMA AI works through it step by step. SOMA builds the model after every change, and SOMA AI looks at pictures of its own result to check it. In the video this took about 39 minutes.

The result is a round tower, 113.8 mm in diameter and 114 mm tall: the tower, a top cover, the front grille, the base and the white light ring, plus standard screws and heat-set inserts. The board and the speaker stay inside as references.

image.alt: The finished smart speaker case in SOMA: a round dark tower with a white light ring on top and a speaker grille in front, next to SOMA AI's summary with the adjustable parameters

steps.title: Check that everything fits
text: Click Section above the 3D view to cut the case open. These tools only change the view, not the model. In the video the board sits right under the top, and the speaker right behind its grille.
Click Explode to pull the parts apart and see how the case goes together: the light ring and the cover on top, the grille in front, the base below, all held by screws in heat-set inserts.

image.alt: Section through the case along X: the board under the top with the light ring, the speaker behind the grille, and the Section panel at the bottom left

steps.title: Show a change with Mark up
text: To hang the speaker on the wall, turn the model to the back, click Mark up and draw the keyhole where you want it: in the video a circle for the screw head, a slot above it, an arrow and a short note.

Send to agent puts the picture into SOMA AI's input. Add one sentence and send it. After about 14 minutes the keyhole is on the back, right where it was drawn: an 8.8 mm head opening and a 4.6 mm neck, reinforced on the inside.
steps.prompt: Add a keyhole slot here, so I can hang the speaker on a screw in the wall.

image.alt: Mark up on the back of the case: a keyhole drawn in orange with an arrow and the note keyhole for a wall screw, and the Send to agent button at the bottom right

steps.title: Change sizes with sliders
text: Because the prompt asked for parameters, the main sizes are in the Parameters tab on the left: in the video the wall thickness, the grille hole width and the overall height.
Open a row and drag its slider, and SOMA rebuilds the model, without the AI. Reset all brings back SOMA AI's values.

image.alt: The Parameters tab with Wall thickness set to 2.8 mm on a slider from 2 to 3.2 mm, Grille hole width 3.2 mm and Overall height 114 mm, next to the case

steps.title: Export for your slicer
text: Click Export, keep All parts and choose 3MF. You get one file per printed part, ready for the slicer. The board, the speaker and the screws stay out.

image.alt: The Export menu with All parts selected and the 3D printing formats STL, 3MF and AMF highlighted, labeled 3MF or STL for the slicer

tips: Place the parts first, then design the case. When the board and speaker sit where you want them, SOMA AI has a fixed frame to design around.
The real file beats your description. In the video the prompt asked for posts at four holes; SOMA AI noticed that the board has only three mounting holes and used all three.
Mention everything you need to reach from outside: buttons, ports, LEDs, microphones, cables. What you do not mention may end up closed.
End a long request with "Ask me about anything that is unclear before you start." SOMA AI then asks its questions at once, before it spends time on the model.

This was a simple example, made quickly. With more time and planning you can go much further: the end of the video shows a detailed smart speaker with a fabric cover held by piping, several circuit boards and an LED ring, also designed in SOMA and built.
For general printing rules for cases (wall thickness, clearances, screws, lids), see the guide How to design a 3D printed enclosure with AI.

faq.q: Where do I find a 3D model of my circuit board?
faq.a: Look on the manufacturer's product page or wiki, often under Resources, Downloads or CAD files. Many makers of development boards publish a STEP file for exactly this use, designing a case around the board. If you designed the board yourself, your PCB design program can usually export a STEP file.

faq.q: What if a part has no 3D file?
faq.a: Use its datasheet. A dimensioned drawing in the datasheet is enough for the AI to build a simple stand-in with the right outer size and mounting holes. In the video the speaker was built this way from its datasheet. Check those dimensions against the real part before you print.

faq.q: Will the circuit board end up in my print files?
faq.a: No. In SOMA the board and other imported parts are references: they are shown see-through so the case can be designed around them, but exporting all parts leaves them out, and the standard screws too. Only the printed parts of the case become files.

faq.q: How do I know the board fits before I print?
faq.a: Cut the model open with a section view and look at the board on its posts, the connectors in their openings and the gaps around them. Use Measure for the openings that matter. For a large case, print a small test piece first, for example the part with the ports.

faq.q: How long does SOMA AI take?
faq.a: In the video SOMA AI took about 3 minutes to place the parts, 39 minutes for the case and 14 minutes for the keyhole. The video shows its work sped up. You can watch it work, or do something else in the meantime.

faq.q: Can I change the case later without the AI?
faq.a: Yes, for the values SOMA AI turned into parameters, such as wall thickness, grille hole width or height. You change them with sliders in the Parameters tab and the model rebuilds. For anything else, describe the change or draw it on the model with Mark up and send it to SOMA AI.
